passage.text:
Workshop reminder
Your carpentry workshop starts at nine on Sunday. Please wear closed shoes and tie back long hair. We provide wood and tools; you only need to bring a notebook for measurements.

Notice on the door
The Saturday bread-making class is full. A second session has been added on Sunday at two. Sign up at reception or online. Ingredients are included in the price.

Email from the tutor
Hi everyone, the sewing workshop has moved to Room 3 because the heating in Room 1 is broken. Same time, same day. Bring the fabric you chose last week. Machines are provided.

Library poster
Free introductory first-aid session this Saturday, ten to twelve. No experience needed. Places are limited to twenty, so register by Thursday. Certificates are not included but notes will be emailed.

Text from Anna
The gardening workshop is cancelled this weekend because of frost. The tutor says we should wait until next Saturday when the soil is warmer. Same place, same time. Bring gloves if you have them.

questions.prompt: What must people do by Thursday?

passage.text: The people below want to choose from practical weekend workshops and short courses. Decide which option is most suitable.

passage.label: A
passage.text: Beginner bread baking in a village kitchen — By Sunday afternoon, participants will have baked two loaves and a batch of rolls to take home. A professional baker explains kneading, proving and shaping in a warm kitchen beside the village hall. Flour and equipment are supplied; learners bring an apron and a bag for leftovers. The class runs from ten to three with a lunch break.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Saturday bike maintenance for nervous cyclists — Worried about fixing a puncture on a quiet road? This hands-on session covers tyre changes, brake adjustments and chain care. A patient mechanic guides groups of six in a covered yard near the station. Bring your own bike; tools and spare parts are provided. The workshop lasts two hours and costs very little.

passage.label: C
passage.text: Weekend furniture restoration at the makerspace — If you have an old chair or table gathering dust, bring it along and learn to sand, repair and refinish it. The makerspace supplies sandpaper, clamps and stains; participants bring the item and old clothes. Sessions run both Saturday and Sunday from ten to four. Some experience with hand tools helps but is not essential.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Introduction to home electrics for new homeowners — People who have recently bought a property often feel unsure about changing a plug or fitting a light. This Saturday course covers safe basics in a training flat downtown. A certified electrician supervises groups of eight. Materials and practice boards are included; no tools needed. The fee is moderate and includes a safety handbook.

passage.label: E
passage.text: Sunday morning vegetable gardening for flat dwellers — On the rooftop terrace above the community centre, participants learn to grow herbs, salad leaves and tomatoes in containers. A gardener demonstrates potting, watering and seasonal planning. Compost and seedlings are provided; attendees take their planted pots home. The session is free and runs from nine to eleven.

passage.label: F
passage.text: Drop-in phone photography tips at the park — Just arrive at the bandstand at ten on Saturday with any phone — no booking, fees or experience needed. A photographer shares five quick techniques for better outdoor shots, then the group walks the park practising together. The session ends at twelve; participants keep all photos on their own devices.

passage.label: G
passage.text: Two-day beginner sewing and alterations course — Over one full weekend, learners master hemming, button replacement and simple pattern reading. The tutor provides machines and thread; participants bring fabric or an item to alter. Classes run ten to four both days in a bright studio near the market. The course fee covers all consumables and a takeaway repair kit.

passage.label: H
passage.text: Evening candle making with natural ingredients — Come and discover how to pour soy candles scented with essential oils. This relaxed Friday-evening workshop suits anyone wanting a creative gift or a new hobby. All materials are supplied and each participant leaves with two finished candles. The studio is upstairs, so step-free access is not available.

Tom has just bought his first house and feels nervous about basic electrical jobs. He can attend on Saturday and prefers a course with a certified instructor and included materials.
Sofia has an old wooden chair she wants to restore. She is free all weekend, does not mind wearing messy clothes and has used hand tools before.
Ben cycles to work but panics when something goes wrong. He wants a short, cheap session where he can practise on his own bike with expert guidance nearby.

parts.passageTitle: Part 3 – Learning to build with my hands

passage.text: I signed up for a weekend carpentry course almost by accident. A friend mentioned it over lunch, and I thought it would be a pleasant way to spend a Saturday. I had never held a proper saw before, and I assumed everyone else would be experienced. When I arrived, though, I discovered that most of the twelve participants were complete beginners like me, and our tutor, a cheerful woman named Helen, made us feel welcome immediately.

The first morning was surprisingly difficult. Helen showed us how to measure and cut a simple joint, but my hands shook and the wood split twice. She laughed kindly and said that every carpenter ruins timber at the start. By the afternoon, I had managed a clean cut, and the small shelf I was building began to look like something real. The other learners offered tips and encouragement, and the atmosphere felt more like a group of friends than a classroom.

I left on Sunday evening with a rough but functional shelf and a new respect for people who work with their hands daily. The course did not make me a carpenter, but it taught me that patience matters more than talent. I have since built two more shelves at home, and each one is slightly better than the last. Helen was right: everyone ruins timber at the start.

options.label: Patience matters more than natural talent.

passage.text: I had always wanted to learn the guitar, but I never seemed to find the right moment to start practising. (16) ..... One day, my neighbour offered to teach me a few chords in exchange for help with his English homework, which seemed like a perfect arrangement. My neighbour was a patient teacher who never made me feel stupid when I made mistakes, and he always encouraged me to try again whenever I felt like giving up completely.

My first lesson was much harder than I had expected it to be. (17) ..... My fingers hurt from pressing the strings, and I could not change chords quickly enough to play a complete song without long pauses between them. I practised the same basic chords for hours every day after school, slowly building up strength in my fingers until the strings no longer hurt when I pressed them down.

After a few weeks of regular daily practice, things began to improve noticeably. (18) ..... I could finally play a whole song without stopping, which felt like a real achievement and motivated me to keep going. My parents noticed how determined I had become and bought me a better quality guitar for my birthday, which made a huge difference to the sound I could produce.

My neighbour suggested that I perform at the school talent show in front of everyone. (19) ..... I was absolutely terrified, but I agreed to play a simple piece in front of the audience because I did not want to miss the opportunity. On the night of the show, my hands were shaking as I walked onto the stage, but I took a deep breath and reminded myself that I had practised enough to do this well.

The performance went much better than I had ever hoped it would. (20) ..... Now I am saving up to buy my own electric guitar so I can keep improving and maybe start a band with my friends. The new arrangement made the final evening feel special, because everyone could see how much patient rehearsal had improved the group’s confidence and timing.

parts.passageTitle: Part 6 – Learning to swim as an adult

passage.text: I decided to learn how to swim at the age of twenty-five, which felt quite late. Most of (27) ........ friends had already learned when they were children, so I felt embarrassed about starting. I signed (28) ........ for a beginner class at the local sports centre near my house. The instructor was very patient and never made me (29) ........ rushed or pressured during the lessons. After a few weeks, I could float on my back without (30) ........ help from the instructor at all. The first time I swam a full length of the pool, I felt so proud (31) ........ I phoned my mother immediately to tell her the news. Now I go to the pool twice a week, and I wonder why (32) ........ took me so long to start learning this skill. Learning to swim as an adult taught me that it is never too late to try something new, and I now encourage my friends to take up hobbies they have always been curious about but never tried. The instructor never laughed when I made mistakes. Instead, she explained each movement again, and this patient approach helped me stay calm when I practised without anyone beside me.
